paragraphs: Although the measure for netilat yadayim (ritual handwashing) is a revi'it, one should be careful to pour it abundantly. Those ignorant people who wash but do not wash properly are punished more than those who do not wash at all: first, they eat without proper handwashing, since they have not washed as the law requires; second, they recite a blessing in vain; and third, there is a grievance against them before God: since they wash anyway, why do they not wash properly? What loss is there in it, and what heavy burden does it place upon them? This is nothing but ill will. Therefore, a God-fearing person should be careful and warn others in this matter, to perform the mitzvah properly, as written in Chesed LaAlafim, siman 158 - see there. But although one who eats a kezayit (olive-bulk) is obligated in handwashing, one recites the blessing 'al netilat yadayim' only if one eats a k'veitzah (egg-bulk), which is eighteen dirhams. And if one intended to eat a k'veitzah and blessed on the handwashing, but when it came time to eat did not eat a k'veitzah but only a kezayit, there is no concern here of a blessing recited in vain for having blessed on the handwashing; nevertheless, he should press himself, where possible, to eat a k'veitzah for the sake of the blessing.

clarification.explanation:
Although the measure for netilat yadayim is a revi'it, one should be careful to wash abundantly (with a generous flow of water). Those ignorant people who wash but not properly are punished more than those who do not wash at all, for three reasons: (a) they eat without handwashing, since their washing is not proper according to the law; (b) they recite a blessing in vain; (c) there is "a grievance against them before God" - since they do wash, why not properly? What loss and what burden is there in doing so? This is nothing but ill will. Therefore, one who fears God should be careful and warn others to perform the mitzvah properly (Chesed LaAlafim).
Nevertheless, although one who eats a kezayit is obligated in handwashing, he does not recite "al netilat yadayim" unless he eats a k'veitzah's worth. And if he intended to eat a k'veitzah and blessed on the washing, but ultimately ate only a kezayit - there is no concern of a blessing in vain; nevertheless he should press himself to eat a k'veitzah where possible, in order to fulfill the blessing.
takeaways: One washes the hands abundantly; one who washes improperly is punished severely (eating without proper washing, reciting a blessing in vain, and "a grievance against them before God").
One who eats a kezayit is obligated in handwashing, but recites "al netilat yadayim" only when eating a k'veitzah (and should strive to eat a k'veitzah for the sake of the blessing).

paragraphs: The obligation of netilat yadayim applies to both men and women, and, due to our many sins, there are women who eat without handwashing and do not feel it to be a sin, having made it as though permitted to themselves; and some think that since they do not know how to recite Birkat HaMazon, they therefore should also not bless on handwashing - and one must inform them that the one has nothing to do with the other. Every person must supervise his household in this matter, inform them of its severity, and always caution them; and he should also train his young children, even though they have not yet reached the age of obligation, so that they become accustomed to it from their childhood. And it is written in the manuscript Sefer Keter Malchut: at the last pouring of the handwashing, for each and every hand one should fill his cupped palms with water, as Rav Chisda said (Shabbat 62b): "I filled my cupped hands with water," etc., and at that moment he should have in mind that "mayim" (water) is an acronym for "melo yadeinu mibirkhotekha" ("our hands full of Your blessings"), and he should also have in mind that "mayim" is an acronym for "me'usar matnot yadekha" ("tithed from the gifts of Your hand"). Thus far [his words]. And it is a beautiful custom.

clarification.explanation: The obligation of netilat yadayim applies to both men and women, but unfortunately there are women who eat without handwashing and do not sense that this is a transgression, and some of them mistakenly think that since they do not know how to recite Birkat HaMazon, they need not bless on handwashing either - one must clarify to them that there is no connection between the two. Every person must supervise his household members in this matter, explain to them its seriousness, and caution them always, and likewise train even young children - though they are not yet obligated in the mitzvot - so that they become accustomed from a young age. In the book Keter Malchut (manuscript) it is brought: at the last pouring of the handwashing, one should fill his cupped palm with water (as Rav Chisda said in the Talmud, "I filled my cupped hands with water"), and at that moment have in mind the acronym of the word "mayim" (water): "melo yadeinu mibirkhotekha" ("our hands full of Your blessings"), and also "me'usar matnot yadekha" ("tithed from the gifts of Your hand") - and this is a beautiful custom.
takeaways: The obligation of netilat yadayim applies to women exactly as it does to men, and there is no connection between knowing Birkat HaMazon and the obligation of handwashing.
Young children should be trained in netilat yadayim from an early age, even before they are obligated in the mitzvot.

paragraphs: Anyone who washes and does not turn his hands this way and that during the washing - it is nearly certain that the water does not reach the entire hand, as can be observed by sight. Therefore, one should be careful to turn his hands this way and that during the washing, so that the water reaches the entire hand.

clarification.explanation: One who washes his hands without turning them in every direction during the washing - it is nearly certain that the water does not cover the entire hand, as can be seen by observation. Therefore, one should take care to turn the hands in every direction during the washing so that the water reaches the whole hand.
takeaways: One should turn the hands in every direction while pouring the water, to ensure that the water covers the entire hand.

paragraphs: When one washes, he should take the vessel in his right hand and hand it to his left hand, in order to subdue the left [hand] like a servant entering to serve his master; and then the left hand pours on the right three times in succession, one after another, and he places the vessel on the ground, and the right hand (which has already been washed) takes it up by itself from the ground and pours from it, by means of the left hand, three times in succession; and afterward he rubs the right hand three times in succession, and then rubs the left hand also three times in succession. This is the order set forth explicitly in the siddur of our teacher the RaShash, of blessed memory, who required pouring three times in succession and also rubbing three times; and although from the words of our teacher the holy Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaMitzvot it appears that one should pour twice and rub once, certainly this matter was clarified for our teacher the RaShash from the words of our teacher the Ari elsewhere, for our teacher the RaShash can be trusted not to innovate anything from his own understanding unless he found for it disclosure and proof in the words of our teacher the Ari; therefore one should not deviate from his words, especially since in this matter no harm results from the addition. And I have heard that this is the custom of the community of Chasidim in Beit El: to pour three times in succession and to rub three times in succession.

clarification.explanation: The order of the washing: one takes the vessel in the right hand and passes it to the left hand, in order to subdue the left hand like a servant who enters to serve his master. Then the left hand pours on the right hand three times in succession, and afterward one places the vessel on the ground, and the right hand (already washed) lifts it by itself from the ground and pours on the left hand three times in succession. Afterward one rubs the right hand three times in succession, and then also rubs the left hand three times in succession. This is the order according to the siddur of Rabbi Shalom Sharabi (the RaShash), who required pouring three times and rubbing three times, even though from the words of the holy Ari elsewhere (in the book Sha'ar HaMitzvot) it seems that one should pour only twice and rub once - but certainly Rabbi Shalom Sharabi based his practice on another source in the writings of the Ari, and therefore one should not depart from his words, especially since there is no loss in adding the extra pourings. The custom of the community of Chasidim of Beit El in Jerusalem is to pour three times and rub three times, following the method of the RaShash.
takeaways: The order of the washing: passing the vessel to the left hand, pouring from the left onto the right three times, then from the right onto the left three times, and finally rubbing each hand three times.
The prevailing custom (following the RaShash and the practice of the community of Beit El) is three pourings and three rubbings for each hand.

paragraphs: After netilat yadayim and rubbing, one should raise his hands up to the level of his head, to elevate and raise the aspect of Vav-Heh, which are the secret of the lower waters, so as to clothe them in the aspect of Yud-Heh, which are the upper waters, and to elevate and raise the aspect of the four letters of the Name YHVH so as to clothe them in the aspect of the tip (kotz) of the Yud of the Name Havayah, and to unify them in a complete unification, and to draw forth abundance to his body and his soul and to bind them together. And when he raises his hands up to the level of his head, then immediately he should recite the blessing 'al netilat yadayim,' so that the raising of his hands should not be in vain, as mentioned in the holy Zohar (Balak 198b), that it is forbidden to raise one's hands empty-handed. And after the blessing 'al netilat yadayim,' while his hands are still upright, he should spread his hands to receive abundance and blessing from the ten kinds of bounty that flow to the twelve aspects of holiness included in the ten holy sefirot, alluded to in the ten fingers of his hands, and he should intend to draw from the Ein Sof (Infinite) light of mochin (supernal minds) and bounty to the twelve aspects of holiness alluded to in the ten all-inclusive sefirot, which are the ten kinds of blessings mentioned in the verse, 'And may He give you...' (Bereishit 27:28-29) through 'and blessed be those who bless you.'

clarification.explanation: This chapter is explicitly kabbalistic in content ("secret"): after the handwashing and rubbing, one should raise the hands up to the height of the head, in order to hint at and effect the elevation of the aspect of "Vav-Heh" (the secret of the lower waters) so that it clothes itself in the aspect of "Yud-Heh" (the secret of the upper waters), and to raise the four letters of the Name Havayah and join them to the aspect of the tip of the Yud of that Name, thereby achieving a complete unification and drawing forth abundance to the body and the soul. The moment the hands are raised to the height of the head, one immediately recites the blessing "al netilat yadayim," so that the raising should not be in vain - as it is written in the holy Zohar that it is forbidden to raise the hands without a blessing. After the blessing, while the hands are still raised, one spreads them to receive abundance from the ten kinds of blessing alluded to in the ten fingers (which correspond to the ten holy sefirot and the twelve aspects included within them), intending to draw forth divine abundance and light through the ten kinds of blessing mentioned in the verse "And may God give you... and blessed be those who bless you" (from Isaac's blessing to Jacob).
takeaways: Raising the hands to the height of the head after the washing is done with a kabbalistic intention (secret) of elevation and supernal unification, and immediately afterward one recites the blessing "al netilat yadayim" so that the raising should not be devoid of a blessing.

paragraphs: Our teacher [the Ari], of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'ar HaMitzvot that the measure of netilat yadayim is the whole hand, that is, the five fingers and the palm itself up to the wrist joint, etc. And by this one can understand the matter of netilat yadayim (literally, "the lifting/carrying of the hands"), which is an expression of elevation, as in "and He lifted them and carried them" (Isaiah 63:9); the meaning being that at the time of their washing, one should raise them upward to the level of the head, or at least to the level of the two sides of the face, for the face too is included in the category of "head." And when you raise your hands, you should intend to draw the joints of the arms inward, and they should not protrude and jut out toward the back of the body as is the practice [of some], which are called 'koudes' in the vernacular, alluding to 'and all their backs were turned to the house.' Thus far his words.

clarification.explanation: The holy Ari wrote in the book Sha'ar HaMitzvot that the measure of netilat yadayim is the entire hand - the five fingers and the palm up to the wrist joint. From this one can understand why the act is called "netilat yadayim" - from a term of lifting and carrying, as in the verse "and He lifted them and carried them" - meaning that at the time of washing one should raise the hands upward to the height of the head, or at least to the height of the face (since the face too is considered part of the "head"). When raising the hands, one should intend to draw the elbow joints inward (close to the body), rather than leaving them protruding and turned backward as is customary with some people - alluding to "all their backs were turned to the house" (symbolizing something negative).
takeaways: At the time of washing, one should raise the hands to the height of the head or at least the face, and draw the arms close to the body rather than leaving them protruding backward.

paragraphs: He should recite the blessing 'al netilat yadayim' after the washing, before the drying; and if he did not bless until he began to eat, he should no longer bless. And there is one who says that even if he did not bless until after the drying, he should no longer bless. Therefore one must be careful to bless before the drying, and all the more so it is forbidden for him to bless while he is drying his hands, as is the custom of the common people, for it is forbidden to engage in any matter whatsoever, even the slightest, while one is reciting a blessing, as mentioned in Chesed LaAlafim, siman 158, letter 3, and see Matteh Yosef, part 2, and other later authorities. And accordingly, if he forgot and did not bless before the drying, he should not bless after the drying, due to a doubt regarding blessings. However, the glossator on Chesed LaAlafim there wrote that if he dried his hands before the blessing, he should go back and wash his hands [again] in order to bless before the drying - see there - and he wrote well, and so it is proper to do, so that he not lose the blessing, and there is no concern here of 'causing an unnecessary blessing,' as I have written, please God, elsewhere on this matter; but before he washes [again], he should touch his flesh with his hands and render them impure, and then wash and bless before the drying.

clarification.explanation: One recites the blessing "al netilat yadayim" after the washing and before the drying. And if he did not bless until he began to eat - he should no longer bless; and there is one who says that even if he did not bless until after the drying - he should no longer bless. Therefore one must take care to bless before the drying, and all the more so it is forbidden to bless while drying the hands (as is the practice of the common people), since it is forbidden to engage in any activity at all while reciting a blessing (Chesed LaAlafim). Accordingly, if one forgot to bless before the drying, he should not bless afterward, due to a doubt regarding blessings. However, the glossator on Chesed LaAlafim there wrote that if he dried his hands before the blessing, he should go back and wash again in order to bless before the drying, and so it is proper to do, so as not to lose the blessing (and there is no concern here of "causing an unnecessary blessing"); but before washing again, he should touch his flesh with his hands to render them impure, and then wash and bless before the drying.
takeaways: One recites "al netilat yadayim" after the washing and before the drying; and it is forbidden to bless while drying.

If one forgot to bless before drying, he should not bless afterward (due to a doubt regarding blessings); and it is proper to touch his flesh, wash again, and bless before drying, so as not to lose the blessing.

paragraphs: He should dry his hands well before he breaks bread, for one who eats without drying the hands is considered as if he eats impure bread (Sotah 4b). And there are those who are stringent even when one washes his hands all at once and pours a revi'it over them at once - even so, drying is required before eating. And he should not dry his hands on his robe, for that is likely to cause forgetting [of one's learning].

clarification.explanation: One should dry the hands well before breaking the bread, because eating without drying the hands is considered as if one eats impure bread, as our Sages said. There are those who are stringent about this even when the hands are washed all at once with a revi'it poured in a single pouring - drying is still required before eating. One should not dry the hands on one's robe [garment], since doing so causes forgetfulness (of one's Torah learning).
takeaways: One should dry the hands well before eating, even if the washing itself was done perfectly - and one should not dry them on the garment one is wearing.

paragraphs: If he relieved himself and wants to eat immediately, he should first wash his hands for having relieved himself and recite 'Asher Yatzar,' and afterward touch his hands to the covered parts of his body, and then wash his hands [again] and recite 'al netilat yadayim.' But it is not possible to make one washing serve for both, since the two washings are not equal: the washing for relieving oneself requires three pourings with intervals between them, while the washing for eating requires three pourings in succession, one right after the other. Therefore he should do as we have written. However, if he does not have much water, or he needs to hurry, he may do the following: wash his hands with intervals, three times, intending in this washing also for the sake of eating, and recite the blessing 'al netilat yadayim' and 'HaMotzi'; and after he eats a kezayit of the HaMotzi bread, he should recite 'Asher Yatzar.' But he should not do this except in a case of necessity, for ab initio it is best to perform two separate washings, each according to its own law, as we have written.

clarification.explanation: One who has relieved himself and wants to eat immediately should first wash his hands for having relieved himself and recite "Asher Yatzar," and afterward touch his hands to the covered parts of his body (in order to renew the impurity of the hands), and only then wash his hands again and recite "al netilat yadayim." It is not possible to perform a single washing shared by both needs, because the washings differ from one another: the washing after using the bathroom requires three pourings with pauses between them, whereas the washing for eating requires three pourings in succession, one after another. If there is not much water, or he is in a hurry, he may wash his hands once with three pourings with pauses (as for the bathroom), but intend in this washing also for the sake of eating, and then bless both "al netilat yadayim" and "HaMotzi"; after eating a kezayit of the bread he should bless "Asher Yatzar." But one should act this way only in a case of pressing need - ab initio it is preferable to perform two separate washings, each according to its law.
takeaways: After relieving oneself and wanting to eat immediately - ab initio one performs two separate washings (one for the bodily need and one for eating), and only in a case of pressing need may they be combined into a single washing.

paragraphs: One who eats requires netilat yadayim even if another person places [the food] into his mouth and he himself does not touch the food; and it is forbidden to feed one who does not wash his hands, and likewise it is forbidden to give food to one whom he knows does not recite a blessing. Therefore, a homeowner who brings bread to his household and knows that they do not bless and do not perform netilat yadayim - the yoke of the transgression hangs upon his neck. And likewise, if a poor person comes to his house to request bread, and he knows of him that he does not bless and does not wash his hands, he thereby commits a transgression in the very place of a mitzvah, and over this let the mourners mourn.

clarification.explanation: One who eats requires netilat yadayim even if another person places the food into his mouth and he himself does not touch it. It is forbidden to feed someone who has not washed his hands, and likewise it is forbidden to give food to someone known not to recite a blessing. Therefore, a homeowner who brings bread to his household members and knows they do not bless and do not perform netilat yadayim - the responsibility for the transgression rests upon him. Likewise, if a poor person comes to his house asking for bread, and he knows the person does not bless and does not wash his hands, the one giving the bread thereby commits a transgression even though the act itself (giving charity) is a mitzvah - and over this one ought to grieve.
takeaways: It is forbidden to give food to someone known not to wash his hands and not to bless, even in the case of giving charity or feeding a small child who is fed by another.

paragraphs: It is required that there be in the water a revi'it gathered in one place, that is, twenty-seven dirhams of water, which is the measure of an egg and a half. And if there was not a [full] revi'it in the vessel, and he poured it on his hand, and then went and brought [more] water and completed [the measure] - his hands are impure, and there is no remedy for him except that he dry them, and then pour upon them [again] from a vessel that has a revi'it of water. And every person must pay attention to this matter, for it is common and frequent that a person, in his innocence, takes the vessel and pours it on his hands thinking that it contains more than a revi'it of water, and after he has poured he realizes that it was less than a revi'it - in that case he should be careful to dry [his hands] first, and afterward wash from water that he brings anew, containing the [proper] measure.

clarification.explanation: There must be, in the water, at least a revi'it (the measure of an egg and a half, that is, twenty-seven dirhams by weight) gathered in one place (in one vessel). If the vessel did not contain a full revi'it, and one poured what was in it onto the hand, and then brought additional water and completed the measure - the hands are still considered impure, and there is no remedy except to dry them first and then wash again from a vessel containing a full revi'it. One should be careful about this, since it commonly happens that a person mistakenly takes a vessel thinking it contains more than a revi'it, and after pouring discovers that it contained less - in such a case he must dry his hands first and then wash again with fresh water containing the required measure.
takeaways: The washing must be performed from a vessel containing a full revi'it of water poured at once - not by combining small amounts from two separate pourings.

paragraphs: One who washes his hands must be careful not to interrupt the flow [of water] until he has washed the whole hand at once, so that the entire hand becomes covered with water, such that not even a small part of it remains without becoming wet with the water. And this matter is quite common: sometimes one pours a great deal of water on the hand, and nevertheless there is found a small spot on the hand where the water did not take hold, which remains completely dry.

clarification.explanation: During the washing, one must be careful not to interrupt the stream of water until the entire hand is covered with water at once, so that not even a small part of the hand remains dry. This is quite common - one pours a great deal of water on the hand and yet a small spot on the hand remains that the water never reached at all.
takeaways: One must ensure that the water truly covers the entire hand during the washing without missing any spot, even when pouring a large quantity of water.

paragraphs: One who washed part of his hand and dried it, and then went back and washed the rest of his hand - his hand is impure as it was before, for there is no [valid] washing for half [a hand], unless upon the part he washed first there remains a moisture sufficient to moisten [something else] ('tofei'ach al menat lehatpi'ach').

clarification.explanation: One who washed only part of his hand and dried it, and then went back and washed the remainder of the hand - his hand is still considered impure as it was, because there is no valid washing for half a hand, unless moisture from the water still remains on the part washed first ("tofei'ach al menat lehatpi'ach" - moist enough to moisten something else).
takeaways: The washing cannot be divided into two stages on the same hand if it was dried in between - unless moisture from the first washing remains.

paragraphs: One who has a wound on his hand with a bandage over it does not need to remove the bandage at the time of washing, and he need only be careful to wash his hands with a revi'it of water all at once; for otherwise, the water that is on the bandage will flow back and render the hand impure. And even though he washed with a [full] revi'it, it is good that he wrap a soft cloth over the bandage on account of the grime - see Eliyah Rabbah. And if in the middle of the meal he removed the bandage, or it fell off, he must go back and wash the whole hand [again], since there is no [valid] washing for half [a hand].

clarification.explanation: One who has a wound on his hand with a bandage over it need not remove the bandage at the time of washing, but he must take care to wash his hand with a revi'it of water all at once - for otherwise, the water absorbed by the bandage will flow back and render the hand impure. Even though he washed properly with a full revi'it, it is good to wrap a soft cloth over the bandage because of the grime it may carry. If, in the middle of the meal, he removed the bandage or it fell off, he must go back and wash the entire hand again, since there is no valid washing for half a hand.
takeaways: One who has a bandage on the hand need not remove it for the washing, but must wash with a revi'it of water at once; and if the bandage is removed or falls off in the middle of the meal, the whole hand must be washed again.

paragraphs: If he washed his hands, and when he came to rub them he saw that a spot remained on his palm to which the water had not clung and which remained dry, and no water remained in the vessel, and it was also not possible to bring [water] from elsewhere in order to wash a second time - he should be careful not to rub [his hands], for if he rubs he will render his entire hand impure on account of that spot that remained without water; and he should wait until it dries by itself, and not dry it with a towel. And thereby he discharges his obligation of washing, according to the opinion of those who hold that it suffices [to wash] up to the fingers; and although we do not rule according to that opinion, in such a case we rely on it, since it is a time of pressing need to eat bread by means of this washing, as it is not possible for him to rectify the matter. But he should not recite the blessing 'al netilat yadayim' with [God's] Name and Sovereignty, but rather recite it without Name and Sovereignty, and merely have Name and Sovereignty in mind - see Chesed LaAlafim 162:3.

clarification.explanation: One who washed his hands, and upon coming to rub them discovered that a spot remained on the palm that the water had not reached at all, and there was no water left in the vessel and no way to bring water from elsewhere in order to wash again - must be careful not to rub the hand, since rubbing would render the entire hand impure because of that dry spot. Instead, he should wait for the hand to dry by itself (not drying it with a towel), and thereby fulfills the obligation of washing according to the opinion that holds it suffices to wash up to the fingers - although the halacha is not decided that way, in such a case, being a time of pressing need with no other option, one may rely on it in order to eat bread. However, he should not recite "al netilat yadayim" with [God's] Name and Sovereignty - rather, he should say the blessing aloud without Name and Sovereignty ("who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning netilat yadayim"), and merely have the Name and Sovereignty in mind.
takeaways: If a dry spot remains on the hand and there is no way to wash again, one does not rub the hands (so as not to render the entire hand impure) and waits for it to dry by itself, reciting the blessing aloud without Name and Sovereignty, while having the Name and Sovereignty in mind.

paragraphs: If he washed one hand and touched it to its counterpart that he had not yet washed, or if another person who had not washed his hands touched him, and even if a day-old infant touched him with its hands - [his hands] have become impure, and the washing does not avail him, except that he must first dry them and then wash them again; but he should not bless a second time. And even one who washed both his hands but was not careful to pour a [full] revi'it on each hand at once, and then rubbed one hand against the other - his hands have become impure, and there is no remedy for him except to dry them and go back and wash them again without a blessing.

clarification.explanation: One who washed one hand and then touched it to the other hand that had not yet been washed, or was touched by another person who had not washed his hands (even a day-old infant) - his hands become impure again, and the earlier washing avails nothing; he must first dry his hands and then wash them again, but without reciting the blessing a second time. Even one who washed both hands but was not careful to pour a full revi'it on each hand at once, and then rubbed one hand against the other - his hands become impure, and there is no remedy except to dry them and go back and wash again without a blessing.
takeaways: Touching an unwashed hand (even that of an infant) nullifies a washing already performed - one must dry the hands and wash again, but without reciting the blessing again.

paragraphs: There are pious men and men of [good] deeds who are meticulous that they do not wash themselves, but rather have another person pour [the water] on their hands, because sometimes, if he did not pour a revi'it on one hand, then when he comes to put water on the other hand he will need to lower his hand, and then the water beyond the wrist joint flows back and renders the hand impure; and furthermore they are concerned lest, in passing the vessel from hand to hand, the washed hand touch the unwashed hand and become impure; and furthermore they are concerned about moisture [on the vessel] that became impure through contact with the unwashed hand, and which afterward renders the washed hand impure when it grasps the handle of the vessel. Therefore, one who is compelled to wash by himself should take care to guard against all these concerns, so that he not err in them; and regarding the last concern, which is on account of the moisture on the vessel, he should be careful to grasp it the second time in a new place; and if this is not possible for him, one may rely on the lenient authorities who say that the water on the handle of the vessel or on its walls does not render impure through the touch of an unwashed hand, for so we hold according to the halacha, as mentioned in Chesed LaAlafim, letter 5.

clarification.explanation: There are pious and meticulous people who are careful not to wash themselves, but rather have another person pour the water on their hands - out of three concerns: (a) that sometimes, if a revi'it was not poured on one hand, then when water is put on the other hand he will need to lower his hand, and the water beyond the wrist joint will flow back and render the hand impure; (b) lest, in passing the vessel from hand to hand, the washed hand touch the unwashed hand and become impure; (c) concern about moisture on the vessel that became impure by touching the unwashed hand, which afterward renders the washed hand impure when it grasps the handle of the vessel. Therefore, one who is compelled to wash by himself should take care to guard against all these concerns; and regarding the last concern (the moisture on the vessel), he should be careful to grasp it in a new spot the second time, and if that is not possible, one may rely on the lenient opinion that the water on the handle or walls of the vessel does not render impure through the touch of an unwashed hand, since so we hold according to the halacha (Chesed LaAlafim).
takeaways: There are meticulous people who have someone else pour the water for them, out of concern that washing by oneself may render the hands impure again (by lowering the hand, hand touching hand, or moisture on the vessel).

One who washes by himself should guard against these concerns; regarding the moisture on the vessel, he should grasp it in a new spot the second time, and if that is not possible, he may rely on the lenient opinion.

paragraphs: One who was in the desert or in a place of danger and has no water must wrap his hands in a cloth in order to eat bread. And if he will certainly find water within a distance of an hour and a quarter's walk, he should wait and not eat. Therefore, if he is walking along the road and wants to eat and has no water: if there is water ahead of him within a distance of an hour and a quarter's walk, he should wait and not eat until he reaches there and washes; and if there is no water ahead of him at all, but it is behind him, if it is a distance of a quarter of an hour's walk, he should trouble himself and go back to wash his hands in order to eat; and if it is more than a quarter of an hour, he is not obligated to go back for this. And that which we say [the rule of] a quarter of an hour's [walk requiring one to] return - this applies where there is no fear or apprehension of danger; but in a case of fear or apprehension of danger, or if he is traveling with a caravan that will not wait for him, in all such cases he should wrap his hands in a cloth and eat the bread.

clarification.explanation: One who is in the desert or in a place of danger and has no water must wrap his hands in a cloth in order to eat bread. If he knows for certain that he will find water within a distance of an hour and a quarter's walk, he should wait and not eat. Therefore, one walking along the road who wants to eat and has no water: if there is water ahead within an hour and a quarter's walk, he should wait and not eat until he arrives there and washes; if there is no water ahead at all, but there is water behind him within a quarter of an hour's walk, he should trouble himself to go back and wash his hands in order to eat; if it is more than a quarter of an hour, he is not obligated to go back for this. This rule of returning for a distance of a quarter of an hour applies only where there is no fear or danger; but in a case of danger, or when traveling with a caravan that will not wait for him, in every such case he should wrap his hands in a cloth and eat the bread without washing.
takeaways: One who has no water while traveling must gauge the distance to the nearest water (ahead or behind) and act according to these rules; but in a case of danger, or with a caravan that will not wait, he should wrap his hands in a cloth and eat without washing.

paragraphs: Before he washes his hands in order to eat bread, he should be careful to say: 'Leshem yichud Kudsha Berich Hu...' ('For the sake of the union of the Holy One, Blessed be He...') 'Behold, I come to fulfill the positive rabbinic commandment to wash my hands and rub them well before the meal, in order to give satisfaction to my Creator and to fulfill the will of my Maker, to rectify the root of this mitzvah in a supernal place; and may it be Your will, O Lord my God and God of my fathers, that this mitzvah of netilat yadayim and rubbing before the meal be considered, accepted, and favored before You, as though I had intended all the proper intentions; and by the merit of the mitzvah of the blessing that we shall recite on netilat yadayim before the meal, may this now be a time of favor before You, and may there flow from the Ein Sof (Infinite) light abundant mochin (supernal minds) and great lights to the twelve countenances alluded to in the ten all-inclusive sefirot, which are alluded to in the ten fingers of the hands, and from there may we receive the abundance of the ten blessings, as it is written: "And may God give you" (drawing forth from the Infinite, mochin and abundance) "of the dew of heaven" (Chochmah) "and of the fatness of the earth" (Binah) "and abundance of grain" (Da'at) "and wine" (Chesed), "let peoples serve you" (Gevurah) "and nations bow down to you" (Tiferet), "be lord" (Netzach) "over your brothers" (Hod), "and let your mother's sons bow down to you" (Yesod); "cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you" (Malchut).'

clarification.explanation: Before washing the hands to eat bread, it is good to recite a short "Leshem Yichud" prayer (a kabbalistic formula - "secret"), in which one accepts upon himself the fulfillment of the rabbinic commandment to wash and rub the hands well before the meal, with the intention of giving satisfaction to the Creator and fulfilling His will, to rectify the root of this mitzvah in the supernal sources, and asks that the mitzvah be considered, accepted, and favored, as though performed with all the proper intentions. The text continues, asking that by the merit of the blessing recited over the washing, great divine abundance and light flow forth, through the ten sefirot alluded to in the ten fingers of the hands, and that from there should come the abundance of the ten kinds of blessing mentioned in Isaac's blessing to Jacob: "And may God give you of the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, and abundance of grain and wine; let peoples serve you and nations bow down to you; be lord over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow down to you; cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you."
takeaways: It is good to recite a short "Leshem Yichud" prayer before netilat yadayim, expressing an inner, kabbalistic intention (secret) for the fulfillment of the mitzvah and for drawing forth abundance and blessing.
